exercises.objective: Explain when sampling methods are needed instead of direct computation.
exercises.prompt: Computing an expectation $\mathbb{E}_p[f(x)] = \int f(x)p(x)\,dx$ exactly requires solving that integral in closed form. Explain a realistic situation where this isn't possible, and how sampling ($\mathbb{E}_p[f(x)] \approx \frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S f(x_s)$, $x_s\sim p$) sidesteps the problem.
hints: Many useful $p$ and $f$ combinations (high-dimensional distributions, complicated non-linear $f$, distributions only known up to normalization) have no closed-form integral, even though $p$ and $f$ are individually easy to evaluate pointwise.

Sampling replaces 'solve the integral' with 'draw many samples from $p$ and average $f$ over them', which only requires being able to *sample from* $p$ (or evaluate it pointwise, for rejection/importance sampling) and evaluate $f$, not integrate anything symbolically.

By the law of large numbers, the sample average converges to the true expectation as $S\to\infty$, so this gives an approximate but computable answer to a problem that might have no closed form at all.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you can't easily sample from $p$ directly, but can sample from a different, more convenient distribution $q$ (with $q(x)>0$ wherever $p(x)>0$). Derive the importance sampling identity $\mathbb{E}_p[f(x)] = \mathbb{E}_q\left[f(x)\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right]$, starting from the definition $\mathbb{E}_p[f(x)] = \int f(x)p(x)\,dx$.
hints: Multiply and divide the integrand by $q(x)$ (valid since $q(x)>0$ wherever the integral has support): $\int f(x)p(x)\,dx = \int f(x)\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}q(x)\,dx$.
Now look at the right-hand side: it's an integral of some function, $f(x)\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$, weighted by $q(x)$.

That's exactly the definition of $\mathbb{E}_q\left[f(x)\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right]$: an expectation under $q$ of the quantity $f(x)p(x)/q(x)$. So $\mathbb{E}_p[f(x)] = \mathbb{E}_q[f(x)p(x)/q(x)]$, letting you estimate an expectation under $p$ using only samples from $q$, reweighted by the **importance weight** $p(x)/q(x)$.

exercises.objective: Compute importance weights and verify the importance sampling identity on a discrete example.
exercises.prompt: Let target $p=[0.2,0.5,0.3]$ and proposal $q=[0.4,0.2,0.4]$ over $x\in\{1,2,3\}$. Compute the importance weight $w(x)=p(x)/q(x)$ for $x=2$. Enter a decimal.
hints: The importance weight is just the ratio of the target probability to the proposal probability, evaluated at the specific value of $x$.
